idiom_name: arr.length = n (truncate) / arr = arr.slice(0, n) (right-sized copy); typed arrays: slice, not subarray
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no capacity layer - the engine's backing store is invisible and unmanaged by the program - so the pattern reduces to the two operations that do exist. Truncation is the in-place half: 'Setting length to a value smaller than the current length truncates the array - elements beyond the new length are deleted' (arr.splice(n) is the method equivalent), which drops the removed references so the engine can reclaim the elements, though actually shrinking the backing store is an engine implementation detail rather than a contract. Releasing bytes for real needs a right-sized copy: arr.slice(0, n) allocates a new array; for binary data, Uint8Array.prototype.slice copies into a buffer of exactly n bytes while subarray returns a view that shares the same ArrayBuffer and frees nothing; on Node, Buffer.from(buf) copies and buffer.transfer() moves an ArrayBuffer to a new size.
pitfalls: subarray() shares the parent ArrayBuffer: a tiny-looking view keeps the whole peak buffer alive and writable - only slice(), Buffer.from or buffer.transfer() make the buffer small.

Truncation is not a promise to hand memory back: engines may keep an over-allocated backing store, and memory is not observable from the language, so length = n is only guaranteed to drop the removed element references.

Rebinding (events = events.slice(0, n)) does not shrink the object anyone else still holds: a closure, another array or a Map/WeakRef entry keeps the peak-sized store alive, and the two sequences then diverge silently.
sources: MDN, Array: length - 'Setting length to a value smaller than the current length truncates the array - elements beyond the new length are deleted', with the writable length attribute and the sparse-array caveats: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/length
